title: Salil Ankola's Journey: From Debuting With Tendulkar to Fighting a Bone Tumour and Severe Depression
excerpt: The former Indian fast bowler, who played his only Test alongside a teenage Sachin Tendulkar, saw his career cut short by a shin tumour at 28 and has recently spoken about his battle with mental health.
body:
• Salil Ankola debuted for India in a Test match at Karachi alongside Sachin Tendulkar, but played just one Test and 20 ODIs in a career plagued by injuries.
  • A bone tumour on his shin forced him out of cricket at 28, cutting short a first-class career of 181 wickets at an average below 26.
  • After reinventing himself as a TV and film actor — including a role alongside Sanjay Dutt — Ankola returned to cricket as Mumbai's chief selector and later served on India's national selection committee.
  • In 2026, he sought treatment for severe depression and has publicly urged others to overcome the stigma around mental health.

Salil Ankola's cricket career began with the kind of debut most fast bowlers dream about — a Test match at Karachi in the company of a teenage Sachin Tendulkar in late 1989. It ended less than a decade later with a bone tumour on his shin and a body that had stopped cooperating with his ambition.

A Career of Promise and Pain

Mumbai's cricket ecosystem had identified Ankola early. A tall right-arm fast bowler with genuine pace and hostility, he was touted as a future spearhead for India in the mould of Kapil Dev. His Test debut against Pakistan yielded two wickets, but it would be his only appearance in whites for India.

In ODIs, Ankola played 20 matches and took 13 wickets, with a best of 3/33 against South Africa in 1993. He was part of India's squad for the 1996 World Cup, though he bowled just five overs in a single match against Sri Lanka at Delhi. Fitness issues kept cycling him in and out of contention, according to CricToday.

At the domestic level, the numbers told a different story. Across 54 first-class matches, Ankola claimed 181 wickets at an average below 26, including eight five-wicket hauls and a best of 6/47. He worked with former England fast bowler Frank Tyson — who was involved with Mumbai's pace-bowling development program — to alter his action and shorten his run-up in an effort to manage the physical toll.

"I'm much better and at peace. I would urge people struggling with depression to seek professional help rather than allow the stigma surrounding mental health to prevent them from speaking about it."

— Salil Ankola, in an interview with HT City, July 2026

The End at 28

By 1997, a bone tumour on his shin ended what was left of Ankola's playing career. He was 28 — an age when most fast bowlers are approaching their peak. In an era when Javagal Srinath held down India's lead pace role and the likes of Manoj Prabhakar and Venkatesh Prasad competed for spots, Ankola never got the sustained run he needed.

Reinvention: Actor, Selector, Survivor

After cricket, Ankola moved into acting. His biggest film role came alongside Sanjay Dutt in the 2000 movie Kurukshetra. He appeared in multiple television serials and was part of the first season of Bigg Boss. The transition was unusual for an Indian cricketer at the time, but Ankola made it work across two decades in entertainment.

Cricket eventually pulled him back. In 2020, the Mumbai Cricket Association appointed him chief selector, and from early 2023 to August 2024 he served on India's senior men's national selection committee before stepping down.

The Toughest Battle

More recently, Ankola has faced what he described as his hardest fight yet. In 2026, he was admitted to a mental health care centre near Pune for treatment of severe depression, triggered by his mother's death and other personal difficulties, according to Hindustan Times. In a July interview with HT City, Ankola said the treatment had helped considerably and urged others to seek professional help without shame.

His willingness to speak openly about depression — still stigmatized in Indian cricket and Indian society more broadly — has drawn support from former teammates and fans. For the diaspora, Ankola's story is a reminder that the athletes they watched growing up faced battles far beyond the boundary.
